title: हिंसामुक्त समाज निर्माण : महिला स्वास्थ्य र सुरक्षाको सवाल
content:
हरेक वर्ष नोभेम्बर २५ लाई अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय महिला हिंसा अन्त्य दिवसका रूपमा मनाइन्छ । यसै दिनदेखि डिसेम्बर १० अर्थात् अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मानव अधिकार दिवससम्म विश्वभर लैङ्गिक हिंसाविरुद्धको १६ दिने अभियान सञ्चालन गरिन्छ । महिलामाथि हुने सबै प्रकारका हिंसा अन्त्य गर्ने, पीडित तथा प्रभावितको अधिकार सुनिश्चित गर्ने र हिंसामुक्त समाज निर्माण गर्ने उद्देश्यले यो अभियान सञ्चालन हुँदै आएको छ । ‘लैङ्गिक हिंसा अन्त्यका लागि एक्येबद्धता : पीडितको संरक्षण, दण्डहीनताको अन्त्य र न्यायको सुनिश्चितता’ भन्ने नाराका साथ यस वर्षकाे अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय महिला हिंसा अन्त्य दिवस मनाइदै छ । यी नाराहरू केवल औपचारिक कार्यक्रमका लागि तयार गरिएका शब्द होइनन् । यी त समाजमा विद्यमान हिंसा, विभेद, अन्याय र मौनताविरुद्ध उठ्नुपर्ने सामूहिक आवाज हुन् । महिलाहरुमाथि हुने हिंसा : देखिने घाउभन्दा गहिरो हुन्छ नदेखिने पीडा महिला हिंसा भन्नासाथ धेरैलाई कुटपिट, शारीरिक आक्रमण वा बलात्कारजस्ता घटनाको मात्र स्मरण हुन्छ। तर महिला हिंसा यतिमा मात्र सीमित छैन । शारीरिक, मानसिक, भावनात्मक, यौनजन्य, आर्थिक, सामाजिक तथा डिजिटल माध्यमबाट हुने दुर्व्यवहार र शोषण पनि लैङ्गिक हिंसाकै स्वरूप हुन् । हाम्रो समाजमा आज पनि धेरै महिलाहरू आफ्नै घरभित्र असुरक्षित जीवन बिताउन बाध्य छन् । श्रीमान् वा परिवारका सदस्यबाट हुने कुटपिट, गालीगलौज, अपमान, शङ्का, धम्की, इच्छाविपरीत यौनसम्बन्ध राख्न बाध्य पार्ने व्यवहार तथा आर्थिक नियन्त्रण घरेलु हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् । कहिलेकाहीँ हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्ति परिवारकै सदस्य, आफन्त, चिनजानको व्यक्ति वा समाजमा प्रतिष्ठित मानिएको व्यक्ति पनि हुन सक्छ। त्यसैले हिंसा केवल अपरिचित व्यक्तिबाट मात्र हुन्छ भन्ने सोच गलत हो । त्यस्तै, कार्यस्थलमा हुने यौन दुर्व्यवहार, असमान व्यवहार, समान कामको असमान पारिश्रमिक, अवसरबाट वञ्चित गराउने प्रवृत्ति, सार्वजनिक स्थानमा हुने दुर्व्यवहार र महिलाको चरित्रमाथि प्रश्न उठाउने सामाजिक व्यवहार पनि महिलाको स्वतन्त्रता र सम्मानमाथिका प्रहार हुन् । प्रविधिको विकाससँगै महिलामाथि हुने हिंसाका स्वरूप पनि परिवर्तन भएका छन्। सामाजिक सञ्जालमार्फत चरित्रहत्या गर्ने, अश्लील तथा आपत्तिजनक सन्देश पठाउने, अनुमति नलिई निजी तस्बिर सार्वजनिक गर्ने, फोटो तथा भिडियो दुरुपयोग गर्ने, अनलाइन धम्की दिने र साइबर बुलिङ गर्ने घटनाहरू बढ्दो चिन्ताको विषय बनेका छन् । अझै पनि बालविवाह, दाइजो प्रथा, छाउपडी, बोक्सीको आरोप, मानव बेचबिखन, जबर्जस्ती विवाह तथा छोरा र छोरीबीच गरिने विभेदले महिलाको जीवन, स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा र आत्मसम्मानमा गम्भीर असर पारिरहेका छन् । हिंसा सहनु महिलाको बाध्यता होइन, हिंसा गर्नु अपराध हो हिंसामा परेका महिलाहरू किन बोल्दैनन् ? किन न्याय खोज्न अगाडि आउँदैनन् ? भन्ने प्रश्न समाजले बारम्बार उठाउँछ । तर उनीहरूको मौनताभित्र लुकेका बाध्यता बुझ्ने प्रयास कमै गरिन्छ । परिवार टुट्ने डर, आर्थिक परनिर्भरता, बालबालिकाको भविष्यको चिन्ता, सामाजिक प्रतिष्ठा गुम्ने भय, माइती तथा आफन्तबाट साथ नपाउने अवस्था, समाजले लगाउने लाञ्छना र न्याय प्राप्त गर्न लाग्ने समय तथा प्रक्रियाको जटिलताले धेरै महिलालाई हिंसा सहेर बस्न बाध्य बनाउँछ । कतिपय महिलाले आफ्नै पीडा व्यक्त गर्दा उल्टै दोषी ठहरिनुपर्छ । उनीहरूको पहिरन, व्यवहार, बोलचाल, चरित्र र व्यक्तिगत जीवनमाथि प्रश्न उठाइन्छ । हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिभन्दा हिंसामा परेकी महिलालाई नै समाजले स्पष्टीकरण माग्ने अवस्था अझै विद्यमान छ । हामीले बुझ्नुपर्छ, हिंसाको जिम्मेवारी हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिको हो, पीडितको होइन । कुनै पनि महिलाको पहिरन, स्वतन्त्रता, व्यक्तिगत निर्णय वा जीवनशैली हिंसाको औचित्य बन्न सक्दैन । न्याय केवल कानुनमा होइन, व्यवहारमा पनि सुनिश्चित हुनुपर्छ महिला हिंसा अन्त्यका लागि कानुन निर्माण गर्नु मात्र पर्याप्त हुँदैन । कानुनको प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयन, निष्पक्ष अनुसन्धान, पीडितमैत्री न्याय प्रणाली, गोपनीयताको संरक्षण र दोषीलाई कानुनअनुसार कारबाही गर्नु उत्तिकै आवश्यक छ । हिंसामा परेका महिलालाई तत्काल सुरक्षा, आवश्यक स्वास्थ्य सेवा, मनोसामाजिक परामर्श, कानुनी सहायता, सुरक्षित आवास र आर्थिक तथा सामाजिक पुनर्स्थापनाको व्यवस्था हुनुपर्छ । पीडितले न्याय खोज्दा बारम्बार आफ्नो पीडा सुनाउनुपर्ने, अपमान सहनुपर्ने वा सामाजिक रूपमा थप प्रताडित हुनुपर्ने अवस्था अन्त्य गरिनुपर्छ। उनीहरूको पहिचान र गोपनीयता सुरक्षित राख्दै सम्मानजनक व्यवहार गर्नु राज्य, सेवा प्रदायक निकाय र समाज सबैको दायित्व हो । यस वर्षको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय नाराले पनि यही सन्देश दिएको छ-पीडितलाई संरक्षण गरौँ, न्याय सुनिश्चित गरौँ र अपराध गर्ने व्यक्तिले उन्मुक्ति पाउने दण्डहीनताको संस्कृतिको अन्त्य गरौँ । महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्न हाम्रो भूमिका के हुन सक्छ ? महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्नु सरकार वा कुनै एक संस्थाको मात्र जिम्मेवारी होइन । परिवार, विद्यालय, समुदाय, सञ्चारमाध्यम, स्थानीय तह, स्वास्थ्य संस्था, सुरक्षा निकाय र प्रत्येक नागरिकको साझा दायित्व हाे। महिलाको सुरक्षा र सम्मान, स्वस्थ समाजको आधार महिला परिवार, समाज र राष्ट्र निर्माणका महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । घरपरिवारको व्यवस्थापनदेखि शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, कृषि, उद्योग, व्यवसाय, प्रशासन, राजनीति र विकासका हरेक क्षेत्रमा महिलाको योगदान अतुलनीय छ । तर विडम्बना, आजको आधुनिक र प्रविधिमैत्री समाजमा समेत महिलाले आफ्नो अस्तित्व, स्वतन्त्रता, सम्मान र सुरक्षाका लागि संघर्ष गर्नुपर्ने अवस्था पूर्ण रूपमा अन्त्य हुन सकेको छैन । महिलामाथि हुने हिंसा केवल कुटपिट, बलात्कार वा शारीरिक आक्रमणमा सीमित छैन। मानसिक यातना, अपमान, आर्थिक नियन्त्रण, सामाजिक विभेद, यौन दुर्व्यवहार, कार्यस्थलमा हुने शोषण र पछिल्लो समय बढ्दै गएको डिजिटल हिंसा पनि यसकै स्वरूप हुन् । विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले महिला हिंसालाई मानव अधिकार उल्लङ्घनका साथै एउटा गम्भीर सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य समस्याका रूपमा व्याख्या गरेको छ । किनकि हिंसाले महिलाको शरीरमा चोट पुर्‍याउने मात्र होइन, मानसिक स्वास्थ्य, यौन तथा प्रजनन स्वास्थ्य, पारिवारिक सम्बन्ध, सामाजिक जीवन र समग्र जीवनको गुणस्तरमा दीर्घकालीन असर पार्दछ। महिला हिंसाको विश्वव्यापी अवस्था : अनुसन्धानले देखाएको वास्तविकता महिला हिंसाको अवस्था बुझ्न विभिन्न राष्ट्रिय तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान र तथ्याङ्क महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले नोभेम्बर २०२५ मा सार्वजनिक गरेको पछिल्लो विश्वव्यापी प्रतिवेदनअनुसार संसारभर करिब ८४ करोड महिला अर्थात् झन्डै तीनमध्ये एक महिलाले आफ्नो जीवनकालमा अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसा अथवा अन्य व्यक्तिबाट हुने यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् । त्यस्तै, पछिल्लो केहि महिनामा यता मात्रै विश्वभर करिब ३१ करोड ६० लाख महिला अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसाबाट प्रभावित भएको अनुमान छ । यी तथ्याङ्कले महिला हिंसा कुनै एक देश, समुदाय वा आर्थिक वर्गको मात्र समस्या नभई विश्वव्यापी स्वास्थ्य तथा मानव अधिकारको चुनौती भएको स्पष्ट पार्छन्। नेपालको अवस्था पनि यसबाट अलग छैन । नेपाल जनसाङ्ख्यिक तथा स्वास्थ्य सर्वेक्षणअनुसार १५ देखि ४९ वर्ष उमेर समूहका २३ प्रतिशत महिलाले १५ वर्षको उमेरपछि कुनै न कुनै प्रकारको शारीरिक हिंसा अनुभव गरेका छन् भने ८ प्रतिशत महिलाले जीवनकालमा यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् । त्यस्तै, श्रीमान् वा अन्तरङ्ग साथीसँग सम्बन्धमा रहेका महिलामध्ये २७ प्रतिशतले शारीरिक, यौनजन्य वा भावनात्मक हिंसाको अनुभव गरेको सर्वेक्षणले देखाएको छ । यी तथ्याङ्क केवल प्रतिशत होइनन्, हाम्रै समाजमा हिंसा र असुरक्षाबीच जीवन बिताउन बाध्य महिलाहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व हुन् । महिला हिंसाका प्रमुख स्वरूपहरू क) शारीरिक हिंसा महिलामाथि गरिने कुटपिट, लात्ती तथा मुक्का प्रहार, जलाउने, घाँटी थिच्ने, चोटपटक पुर्‍याउने, खानपिन वा औषधोपचारबाट वञ्चित गर्ने तथा ज्यान मार्ने धम्की दिने कार्य शारीरिक हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् । विशेषगरी घरभित्र हुने हिंसालाई पारिवारिक विषय भन्दै लुकाउने प्रवृत्तिले धेरै महिला वर्षौँसम्म शारीरिक यातना सहन बाध्य हुन्छन् । यस्ता हिंसाले चोटपटक, हड्डी भाँचिने, आन्तरिक रक्तस्राव, दीर्घकालीन दुखाइ, अपाङ्गता र कतिपय अवस्थामा मृत्युसमेत निम्त्याउन सक्छ । ख) मानसिक तथा मनोवैज्ञानिक हिंसा महिलालाई निरन्तर गाली गर्नु, अपमानित गर्नु, चरित्रमाथि शंका गर्नु, डर देखाउनु, धम्की दिनु, अरूसँग बोल्न तथा भेटघाट गर्न रोक्नु, इच्छाविपरीत निर्णय लाद्नु र आत्मसम्मान कमजोर बनाउने व्यवहार मानसिक हिंसा हुन् । यसको असर बाहिरबाट देखिँदैन, तर भित्रभित्रै महिलाको आत्मविश्वास र मानसिक स्वास्थ्य कमजोर बनाउँदै लैजान्छ । यस्ता महिलामा चिन्ता, अवसाद, तनाव, निद्रासम्बन्धी समस्या र आघातपछिको मानसिक तनाव जस्ता समस्या देखिन सक्छन् । ग) यौनजन्य हिंसा महिलाको इच्छाविपरीत गरिने यौनजन्य व्यवहार, बलात्कार, यौन दुर्व्यवहार, अनिच्छित स्पर्श, यौन शोषण, जबर्जस्ती यौन सम्बन्ध र यौनजन्य धम्की यसका उदाहरण हुन्। यसले अनिच्छित गर्भधारण, यौनजन्य सङ्क्रमण सङ्क्रमणको जोखिम, मानसिक दिऔँ र न्याय सुनिश्चित गरौँ । (लेखक शुक्रराज ट्रपिकल तथा सरूवा रोग अस्पतालमा कार्यरत छिन् ।) Every year, November 25 is observed as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. From this day until December 10, International Human Rights Day, a 16-day campaign against gender-based violence is launched worldwide. This campaign aims to end all forms of violence against women, ensure the rights of victims and affected people, and build a society free from violence. This year's International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is being celebrated with the theme 'Unity to End Gender-Based Violence: Protecting Victims, Ending Impunity and Ensuring Justice'. These themes are not just words prepared for formal events. They are a collective voice that must rise up against the violence, discrimination, injustice and silence that exist in society. Violence against women: The unseen pain is deeper than the visible wound When it comes to violence against women, many people only think of incidents like beatings, physical attacks, or rape. But violence against women is not limited to these. Abuse and exploitation that occur through physical, mental, emotional, sexual, economic, social, and digital means are also forms of gender-based violence. Even today, many women in our society are forced to live unsafe lives within their own homes. Examples of domestic violence include beatings, verbal abuse, humiliation, suspicion, threats, coercive sexual behavior against one's will, and financial control by a husband or family member. Sometimes the perpetrator of violence can be a family member, relative, acquaintance, or even a person considered respected in society. Therefore, it is wrong to think that violence only occurs from strangers. Similarly, sexual harassment in the workplace, unequal treatment, unequal pay for equal work, the tendency to deprive women of opportunities, abuse in public places, and social behavior that questions women's character are also attacks on women's freedom and dignity. With the development of technology, the forms of violence against women have also changed. Incidents of character assassination, sending obscene and offensive messages through social media, publishing private photos without permission, misusing photos and videos, online threats, and cyberbullying have become a matter of growing concern. Child marriage, dowry system, Chhaupadi, witchcraft accusations, human trafficking, forced marriage, and discrimination between sons and daughters still have a serious impact on women's lives, health, education, and self-esteem. It is not a woman's obligation to endure violence, committing violence is a crime. Society repeatedly raises the question of why women who are victims of violence don't speak out? Why don't they come forward to seek justice? But rarely does an effort to understand the hidden compulsions behind their silence occur. Fear of family breakdown, financial dependence, concerns about the future of children, fear of losing social prestige, lack of support from family and relatives, stigmatization by society, and the time and complexity of the process required to obtain justice force many women to endure violence. Some women are accused of expressing their pain. Their dress, behavior, speech, character, and personal lives are questioned. Society still demands an explanation from the woman who is the victim of violence rather than the person who commits the violence. We must understand that the responsibility for violence lies with the perpetrator, not the victim. No woman's dress, freedom, personal decisions, or lifestyle can justify violence. Justice must be ensured not only in law, but also in practice. Enacting laws alone is not enough to end violence against women. Effective implementation of the law, impartial investigations, a victim-friendly justice system, protection of confidentiality, and prosecution of perpetrators according to the law are equally necessary. Women who have been subjected to violence should be provided with immediate protection, necessary health services, psychosocial counseling, legal assistance, safe housing, and economic and social rehabilitation. Victims should not have to repeatedly recount their pain, endure humiliation, or be further socially harassed when seeking justice. It is the responsibility of the state, service providers, and society to protect their identity and privacy and treat them with respect. This year's international slogan also conveys the same message - protect victims, ensure justice, and end the culture of impunity where perpetrators of crimes get away with it. What can be our role in ending violence against women? Ending violence against women is not the sole responsibility of the government or any single organization. It is a shared responsibility of families, schools, communities, media, local levels, health institutions, security agencies, and every citizen. Women's safety and respect, the foundation of a healthy society Women are the important foundation of family, society and nation building. From household management to education, health, agriculture, industry, business, administration, politics and development, women's contribution is unparalleled. But ironically, even in today's modern and technology-friendly society, the situation where women have to struggle for their existence, freedom, respect and security has not been completely eliminated. Violence against women is not limited to beatings, rape, or physical attacks. It also includes mental torture, humiliation, economic control, social discrimination, sexual abuse, workplace exploitation, and the recent rise in digital violence. The World Health Organization has described violence against women as a human rights violation as well as a serious public health problem. Because violence not only harms women's bodies, it also has long-term impacts on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, family relationships, social life, and overall quality of life. The global state of violence against women: The reality revealed by research Various national and international research and statistics are an important basis for understanding the situation of violence against women. According to the latest global report released by the World Health Organization in November 2025, about 840 million women worldwide, or about one in three women, have experienced physical or sexual violence from an intimate partner or sexual violence from another person in their lifetime. Similarly, in the last few months alone, it is estimated that approximately 316 million women worldwide have been affected by physical or sexual violence from intimate partners. These statistics make it clear that violence against women is not just a problem of one country, community, or economic class, but a global health and human rights challenge. Nepal is no different. According to the Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, 23 percent of women aged 15 to 49 have experienced some form of physical violence after the age of 15, while 8 percent have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime. Similarly, the survey showed that 27 percent of women in relationships with their husbands or intimate partners have experienced physical, sexual, or emotional violence. These statistics are not just percentages, they are a representation of the women forced to live amidst violence and insecurity in our society. Main forms of violence against women a) Physical violence Examples of physical violence against women include beating, kicking and punching, burning, strangling, causing injuries, depriving them of food, drink or medication, and threatening to kill them. Many women are forced to endure years of physical abuse, especially due to the tendency to hide domestic violence as a family matter. Such violence can cause injuries, broken bones, internal bleeding, chronic pain, disability, and in some cases even death. b) Mental and psychological violence Constantly insulting, humiliating, questioning a woman's character, instilling fear, threatening, preventing her from speaking to or meeting others, imposing decisions against her will, and behavior that undermines her self-esteem are all forms of mental violence. Its effects are not visible from the outside, but they undermine a woman's self-confidence and mental health from the inside. Such women may experience problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, sleep problems, and post-traumatic stress disorder. c) Sexual violence Examples of this include sexual behavior against a woman's will, rape, sexual abuse, unwanted touching, sexual exploitation, forced sexual intercourse, and sexual intimidation. This can lead to unwanted pregnancies, risk of sexually transmitted infections, psychological trauma, and reproductive health complications. Consent is essential in sexual relations. A woman's right to consent does not end just because she is married. Silence or fear cannot be considered consent. d) Economic violence Taking away the money a woman earns, preventing her from spending her income, depriving her of property rights, preventing her from getting a job, and not participating in financial decisions are examples of economic violence. Economic dependence makes it difficult for women to leave violent relationships. Women's education, employment, skill development, and economic self-reliance are important foundations for preventing violence. e) Social and cultural violence Disappointment at the birth of a girl child, discrimination between sons and daughters, demand for dowry, child marriage, untouchability during menstruation, discrimination against widows and single women, and restrictions on women's freedom are all forms of social violence. There is a need to change the mindset that considers injustice against women in the name of tradition and culture as normal. f) Violence in the workplace Women face various forms of abuse not only at home, but also in hospitals, schools, government offices, private organizations, industries, and other workplaces. Unwanted personal comments, derogatory comments about the body, obscene jokes, unwanted touching, pressure for sexual intercourse, sexual demands under the guise of a job or promotion, and retaliation after reporting are examples of workplace violence. Abuse, especially through abuse of position and power, can weaken women mentally and affect their professional lives. There should be a safe environment in the office, a confidential complaint system, and an impartial investigation. g) Digital violence With the development of technology, the forms of violence against women have also changed. Examples of digital violence include character assassination on social media, sending obscene messages, creating fake accounts, publishing personal photos and videos without permission, online threats, blackmailing, and using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create fake obscene photos and videos. Digital Violence should not be treated as a simple joke or an online dispute. It can seriously affect women's mental health, social reputation, and personal safety. Violence against women and its impact on health From the perspective of health professionals, violence against women is not just a social problem, it is a serious condition that affects the overall health of women. Women affected by violence can experience both immediate and long-term health problems. Physical health: Injuries, broken bones, chronic pain, headaches, digestive system problems, and other physical complications. Mental health: Anxiety, stress, depression, fear, loss of confidence, sleep problems, and suicide risk. Sexual and reproductive health: Unwanted pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, risk of HIV infection, pregnancy complications, and reproductive health problems. Maternal and Child Health: Violence against pregnant women can negatively impact the health of both the mother and the unborn child. It can also affect the mental health, behavior, and academic achievement of children who grow up witnessing violence at home. Research by the World Health Organization has shown that the effects of violence can last long after the incident has ended. Therefore, women affected by violence need not only physical treatment, but also mental health services, psychosocial counseling, and social rehabilitation. The role of healthcare workers: trust and protection along with treatment The role of health workers in the prevention and management of violence against women is very important. A woman who has experienced violence may first go to a hospital or health facility without going to the police or court. She may come to a health facility with injuries, headaches, stomachaches, sleep problems, mental stress, or other health problems. Therefore, healthcare workers must be sensitive to the patient's external symptoms as well as their safety, mental state, and possible background of violence. The following should be prioritized in health services: Communicate with the patient in a safe and confidential environment. Listen carefully to the victim. No accusations or insults of any kind. Perform necessary physical examinations and treatment. Providing mental health and psychosocial support. Provide timely necessary health services in cases of sexual violence. Referral to legal and social protection services as needed. Maintaining patient personal details and confidentiality. The World Health Organization has recommended the LIVES Approach as an initial step in providing support to women affected by violence. L – Listen: Listen carefully. I – Inquire: Understand their needs and concerns. V – Validate: Trust and acknowledge their experience. E – Enhance Safety: Help ensure safety. S – Support: Providing necessary services and support. Its primary purpose is not to control the victim, but to strengthen their confidence, security, and decision-making abilities. A new research-based concept in violence prevention Simply conducting awareness programs is not enough to end violence against women. Research-based policies and programs are needed to prevent it. The RESPECT Women Framework, updated by the World Health Organization in 2025, is an important concept for preventing violence against women. It emphasizes seven key strategies Developing healthy and respectful relationships. Women's empowerment. Ensuring health, legal and social services. Reducing poverty and economic dependence. Making homes, schools and workplaces safe. Preventing abuse of children and adolescents. Changing discriminatory thinking and social norms. This shows that coordination between health, education, economic development, law, and social awareness is necessary to prevent violence against women. Victims need support and justice, not blame. In our society, women who have experienced violence still have to face social humiliation and mental stress in addition to physical pain. In some cases, when a victim makes an incident public, questions are raised about their character, dress, behavior, relationships, and personal life. Questions like why did she go there? Why didn't she file a complaint earlier? Why didn't she end the relationship? Why did she keep quiet? cause further mental anguish to the victim. We need to change the direction of the question. Why did the violence happen? Why weren't the perpetrators brought to justice? Why didn't the victims get timely protection and justice? We should develop a culture of listening to the victim, trusting them, maintaining confidentiality, and providing necessary support, rather than blaming them. Survivor Support, not Victim Blaming, should be our priority. The responsibility of family, society and the state to end violence against women The responsibility to end violence against women is not only women's. It is a shared responsibility of families, men, communities, health institutions, educational institutions, the media, and the state. Daughters and sons should be treated equally in the family. The idea that household chores are the sole responsibility of women should be changed. Women's opinions, decisions, and freedom should be respected. Men should also play an active role in combating violence against women. They should not remain silent when they see humiliation, discrimination, and abuse against women. Health institutions should provide safe, confidential, and victim-friendly services for women affected by violence. Offices and organizations should create a safe work environment and an effective complaint mechanism. The state should prioritize effective implementation of existing laws, impartial investigations, speedy justice, safe havens, free legal aid, and rehabilitation programs.* : Ensuring legal order and justice in Nepal: The Constitution of Nepal, 2072 BS, ensures the rights of women to equality, respect, and security. Similarly, legal provisions such as the Domestic Violence (Offences and Punishments) Act, 2066 BS, the Sexual Harassment at Workplace (Prevention) Act, 2071 BS, and the Criminal Code, 2074 BS have addressed various forms of violence against women and girls. But laws alone are not enough. They must be effectively implemented. Victims should receive fair investigation, a safe environment, health care, legal aid, and timely justice after filing a complaint. The perpetrator of violence, no matter how politically, economically, or socially powerful, cannot be above the law. This year's national slogan also emphasizes the same theme - protecting victims, ending impunity, and ensuring justice. Conclusion: Building a violence-free society is our shared responsibility. The campaign to end violence against women should not be limited to a one-day event or a formal 16-day activity. It is a social campaign that must continue every day, in every home, every office, every school, and every community. We must build a society where families are not disappointed when a girl is born, women do not feel unsafe in their own homes, teenagers do not have to give up their dreams, employees do not have to endure humiliation to keep their jobs, and women who have experienced violence do not have to feel alone when seeking justice. Women's safety is not just a personal need of women, but a criterion for the civilization of society and the development of the nation. As a health worker, I believe that a violence-free environment, safe health care, protection of mental health, and equal rights are the foundations of building a healthy society. Let us all make a common commitment on the occasion of this campaign. Let us not remain silent when we see violence. Let us not blame the victim. Let us not consider injustice normal. Let us not protect the perpetrators of violence. Let us raise our voices in favor of justice and equality. Because the vision of a healthy, prosperous, and civilized society remains incomplete until the safety, respect, and health of women are ensured. Women are not obligated to endure violence. Consent is the basis of every relationship. Women's respect and security are fundamental rights. Victims need not only sympathy, but justice and protection. Perpetrators of violence need legal accountability, not impunity. Let us raise our voices, support the victims, and ensure justice. (The author works at Shukraraj Tropical and Infectious Diseases Hospital.)

दुरुपयोग गर्ने, अनलाइन धम्की दिने र साइबर बुलिङ गर्ने घटनाहरू बढ्दो चिन्ताको विषय बनेका छन् । अझै पनि बालविवाह, दाइजो प्रथा, छाउपडी, बोक्सीको आरोप, मानव बेचबिखन, जबर्जस्ती विवाह तथा छोरा र छोरीबीच गरिने विभेदले महिलाको जीवन, स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा र आत्मसम्मानमा गम्भीर असर पारिरहेका छन् । हिंसा सहनु महिलाको बाध्यता होइन, हिंसा गर्नु अपराध हो हिंसामा परेका महिलाहरू किन बोल्दैनन् ? किन न्याय खोज्न अगाडि आउँदैनन् ? भन्ने प्रश्न समाजले बारम्बार उठाउँछ । तर उनीहरूको मौनताभित्र लुकेका बाध्यता बुझ्ने प्रयास कमै गरिन्छ । परिवार टुट्ने डर, आर्थिक परनिर्भरता, बालबालिकाको भविष्यको चिन्ता, सामाजिक प्रतिष्ठा गुम्ने भय, माइती तथा आफन्तबाट साथ नपाउने अवस्था, समाजले लगाउने लाञ्छना र न्याय प्राप्त गर्न लाग्ने समय तथा प्रक्रियाको जटिलताले धेरै महिलालाई हिंसा सहेर बस्न बाध्य बनाउँछ । कतिपय महिलाले आफ्नै पीडा व्यक्त गर्दा उल्टै दोषी ठहरिनुपर्छ । उनीहरूको पहिरन, व्यवहार, बोलचाल, चरित्र र व्यक्तिगत जीवनमाथि प्रश्न उठाइन्छ । हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिभन्दा हिंसामा परेकी महिलालाई नै समाजले स्पष्टीकरण माग्ने अवस्था अझै विद्यमान छ । हामीले बुझ्नुपर्छ, हिंसाको जिम्मेवारी हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिको हो, पीडितको होइन । कुनै पनि महिलाको पहिरन, स्वतन्त्रता, व्यक्तिगत निर्णय वा जीवनशैली हिंसाको औचित्य बन्न सक्दैन । न्याय केवल कानुनमा होइन, व्यवहारमा पनि सुनिश्चित हुनुपर्छ महिला हिंसा अन्त्यका लागि कानुन निर्माण गर्नु मात्र पर्याप्त हुँदैन । कानुनको प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयन, निष्पक्ष अनुसन्धान, पीडितमैत्री न्याय प्रणाली, गोपनीयताको संरक्षण र दोषीलाई कानुनअनुसार कारबाही गर्नु उत्तिकै आवश्यक छ । हिंसामा परेका महिलालाई तत्काल सुरक्षा, आवश्यक स्वास्थ्य सेवा, मनोसामाजिक परामर्श, कानुनी सहायता, सुरक्षित आवास र आर्थिक तथा सामाजिक पुनर्स्थापनाको व्यवस्था हुनुपर्छ । पीडितले न्याय खोज्दा बारम्बार आफ्नो पीडा सुनाउनुपर्ने, अपमान सहनुपर्ने वा सामाजिक रूपमा थप प्रताडित हुनुपर्ने अवस्था अन्त्य गरिनुपर्छ। उनीहरूको पहिचान र गोपनीयता सुरक्षित राख्दै सम्मानजनक व्यवहार गर्नु राज्य, सेवा प्रदायक निकाय र समाज सबैको दायित्व हो । यस वर्षको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय नाराले पनि यही सन्देश दिएको छ-पीडितलाई संरक्षण गरौँ, न्याय सुनिश्चित गरौँ र अपराध गर्ने व्यक्तिले उन्मुक्ति पाउने दण्डहीनताको संस्कृतिको अन्त्य गरौँ । महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्न हाम्रो भूमिका के हुन सक्छ ? महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्नु सरकार वा कुनै एक संस्थाको मात्र जिम्मेवारी होइन । परिवार, विद्यालय, समुदाय, सञ्चारमाध्यम, स्थानीय तह, स्वास्थ्य संस्था, सुरक्षा निकाय र प्रत्येक नागरिकको साझा दायित्व हाे। महिलाको सुरक्षा र सम्मान, स्वस्थ समाजको आधार महिला परिवार, समाज र राष्ट्र निर्माणका महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । घरपरिवारको व्यवस्थापनदेखि शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, कृषि, उद्योग, व्यवसाय, प्रशासन, राजनीति र विकासका हरेक क्षेत्रमा महिलाको योगदान अतुलनीय छ । तर विडम्बना, आजको आधुनिक र प्रविधिमैत्री समाजमा समेत महिलाले आफ्नो अस्तित्व, स्वतन्त्रता, सम्मान र सुरक्षाका लागि संघर्ष गर्नुपर्ने अवस्था पूर्ण रूपमा अन्त्य हुन सकेको छैन । महिलामाथि हुने हिंसा केवल कुटपिट, बलात्कार वा शारीरिक आक्रमणमा सीमित छैन। मानसिक यातना, अपमान, आर्थिक नियन्त्रण, सामाजिक विभेद, यौन दुर्व्यवहार, कार्यस्थलमा हुने शोषण र पछिल्लो समय बढ्दै गएको डिजिटल हिंसा पनि यसकै स्वरूप हुन् । विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले महिला हिंसालाई मानव अधिकार उल्लङ्घनका साथै एउटा गम्भीर सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य समस्याका रूपमा व्याख्या गरेको छ । किनकि हिंसाले महिलाको शरीरमा चोट पुर्‍याउने मात्र होइन, मानसिक स्वास्थ्य, यौन तथा प्रजनन स्वास्थ्य, पारिवारिक सम्बन्ध, सामाजिक जीवन र समग्र जीवनको गुणस्तरमा दीर्घकालीन असर पार्दछ। महिला हिंसाको विश्वव्यापी अवस्था : अनुसन्धानले देखाएको वास्तविकता महिला हिंसाको अवस्था बुझ्न विभिन्न राष्ट्रिय तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान र तथ्याङ्क महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले नोभेम्बर २०२५ मा सार्वजनिक गरेको पछिल्लो विश्वव्यापी प्रतिवेदनअनुसार संसारभर करिब ८४ करोड महिला अर्थात् झन्डै तीनमध्ये एक महिलाले आफ्नो जीवनकालमा अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसा अथवा अन्य व्यक्तिबाट हुने यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् । त्यस्तै, पछिल्लो केहि महिनामा यता मात्रै विश्वभर करिब ३१ करोड ६० लाख महिला अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसाबाट प्रभावित भएको अनुमान छ । यी तथ्याङ्कले महिला हिंसा कुनै एक देश, समुदाय वा आर्थिक वर्गको मात्र समस्या नभई विश्वव्यापी स्वास्थ्य तथा मानव अधिकारको चुनौती भएको स्पष्ट पार्छन्। नेपालको अवस्था पनि यसबाट अलग छैन । नेपाल जनसाङ्ख्यिक तथा स्वास्थ्य सर्वेक्षणअनुसार १५ देखि ४९ वर्ष उमेर समूहका २३ प्रतिशत महिलाले १५ वर्षको उमेरपछि कुनै न कुनै प्रकारको शारीरिक हिंसा अनुभव गरेका छन् भने ८ प्रतिशत महिलाले जीवनकालमा यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् । त्यस्तै, श्रीमान् वा अन्तरङ्ग साथीसँग सम्बन्धमा रहेका महिलामध्ये २७ प्रतिशतले शारीरिक, यौनजन्य वा भावनात्मक हिंसाको अनुभव गरेको सर्वेक्षणले देखाएको छ । यी तथ्याङ्क केवल प्रतिशत होइनन्, हाम्रै समाजमा हिंसा र असुरक्षाबीच जीवन बिताउन बाध्य महिलाहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व हुन् । महिला हिंसाका प्रमुख स्वरूपहरू क) शारीरिक हिंसा महिलामाथि गरिने कुटपिट, लात्ती तथा मुक्का प्रहार, जलाउने, घाँटी थिच्ने, चोटपटक पुर्‍याउने, खानपिन वा औषधोपचारबाट वञ्चित गर्ने तथा ज्यान मार्ने धम्की दिने कार्य शारीरिक हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् । विशेषगरी घरभित्र हुने हिंसालाई पारिवारिक विषय भन्दै लुकाउने प्रवृत्तिले धेरै महिला वर्षौँसम्म शारीरिक यातना सहन बाध्य हुन्छन् । यस्ता हिंसाले चोटपटक, हड्डी भाँचिने, आन्तरिक रक्तस्राव, दीर्घकालीन दुखाइ, अपाङ्गता र कतिपय अवस्थामा मृत्युसमेत निम्त्याउन सक्छ । ख) मानसिक तथा मनोवैज्ञानिक हिंसा महिलालाई निरन्तर गाली गर्नु, अपमानित गर्नु, चरित्रमाथि शंका गर्नु, डर देखाउनु, धम्की दिनु, अरूसँग बोल्न तथा भेटघाट गर्न रोक्नु, इच्छाविपरीत निर्णय लाद्नु र आत्मसम्मान कमजोर बनाउने व्यवहार मानसिक हिंसा हुन् । यसको असर बाहिरबाट देखिँदैन, तर भित्रभित्रै महिलाको आत्मविश्वास र मानसिक स्वास्थ्य कमजोर बनाउँदै लैजान्छ । यस्ता महिलामा चिन्ता, अवसाद, तनाव, निद्रासम्बन्धी समस्या र आघातपछिको मानसिक तनाव जस्ता समस्या देखिन सक्छन् । ग) यौनजन्य हिंसा महिलाको इच्छाविपरीत गरिने यौनजन्य व्यवहार, बलात्कार, यौन दुर्व्यवहार, अनिच्छित स्पर्श, यौन शोषण, जबर्जस्ती यौन सम्बन्ध र यौनजन्य धम्की यसका उदाहरण हुन्। यसले अनिच्छित गर्भधारण, यौनजन्य सङ्क्रमण सङ्क्रमणको जोखिम, मानसिक आघात तथा प्रजनन स्वास्थ्यमा जटिलता निम्त्याउन सक्छ । यौन सम्बन्धमा सहमति अनिवार्य हुन्छ । विवाह भएको कारणले महिलाको सहमतिको अधिकार समाप्त हुँदैन । मौनता वा डरलाई सहमति मान्न मिल्दैन । घ) आर्थिक हिंसा महिलाले कमाएको पैसा खोस्नु, आफ्नो आम्दानी खर्च गर्न नदिनु, सम्पत्तिको अधिकारबाट वञ्चित गर्नु, रोजगारी गर्न रोक्नु र आर्थिक निर्णयमा सहभागी नगराउनु आर्थिक हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् । आर्थिक परनिर्भरता ले महिलालाई हिंसात्मक सम्बन्धबाट बाहिर निस्कनसमेत कठिन बनाउँछ । महिलाको शिक्षा, रोजगारी, सीप विकास र आर्थिक आत्मनिर्भरता हिंसा रोकथामका महत्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । ङ) सामाजिक तथा सांस्कृतिक हिंसा छोरी जन्मिँदा निराश हुनु, छोरा र छोरीबीच विभेद गर्नु, दाइजो माग्नु, बालविवाह गराउनु, महिनावारी हुँदा छुवाछुत गर्नु, विधवा तथा एकल महिलामाथि विभेद गर्नु र महिलाको स्वतन्त्रतामाथि प्रतिबन्ध लगाउनु सामाजिक हिंसाका स्वरूप हुन् । परम्परा र संस्कृतिको नाममा महिलामाथि हुने अन्यायलाई सामान्य मान्ने सोच परिवर्तन हुन आवश्यक छ। च) कार्यस्थलमा हुने हिंसा महिलाले घरमा मात्र होइन, अस्पताल, विद्यालय, सरकारी कार्यालय, निजी संस्था, उद्योग तथा अन्य कार्यस्थलमा समेत विभिन्न प्रकारका दुर्व्यवहार भोगिरहेका हुन्छन् । अनावश्यक व्यक्तिगत टिप्पणी, शरीरमाथि अपमानजनक टिप्पणी, अश्लील मजाक, अनिच्छित स्पर्श, यौन सम्बन्धका लागि दबाब, जागिर वा पदोन्नतिको प्रलोभन देखाएर यौनजन्य माग गर्नु र उजुरी गरेपछि प्रतिशोध लिनु कार्यस्थलमा हुने हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् । विशेषगरी पद र शक्तिको दुरुपयोगबाट हुने दुर्व्यवहारले महिलालाई मानसिक रूपमा कमजोर बनाउनुका साथै व्यावसायिक जीवनसमेत प्रभावित पार्न सक्छ । कार्यालयमा सुरक्षित वातावरण, गोप्य उजुरी प्रणाली र निष्पक्ष छानबिनको व्यवस्था हुनुपर्छ । छ) डिजिटल हिंसा प्रविधिको आधार हो । महिलाको सम्मान र सुरक्षा मौलिक अधिकार हो । पीडितलाई सहानुभूति मात्र होइन, न्याय र संरक्षण चाहिन्छ । हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिलाई उन्मुक्ति होइन, कानुनी जवाफदेहिता चाहिन्छ । आवाज उठाऔँ, पीडितको साथ दिऔँ र न्याय सुनिश्चित गरौँ । (लेखक शुक्रराज ट्रपिकल तथा सरूवा रोग अस्पतालमा कार्यरत छिन् ।)

हरेक वर्ष नोभेम्बर २५ लाई अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय महिला हिंसा अन्त्य दिवसका रूपमा मनाइन्छ । यसै दिनदेखि डिसेम्बर १० अर्थात् अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय मानव अधिकार दिवससम्म विश्वभर लैङ्गिक हिंसाविरुद्धको १६ दिने अभियान सञ्चालन गरिन्छ । महिलामाथि हुने सबै प्रकारका हिंसा अन्त्य गर्ने, पीडित तथा प्रभावितको अधिकार सुनिश्चित गर्ने र हिंसामुक्त समाज निर्माण गर्ने उद्देश्यले यो अभियान सञ्चालन हुँदै आएको छ ।

‘लैङ्गिक हिंसा अन्त्यका लागि एक्येबद्धता : पीडितको संरक्षण, दण्डहीनताको अन्त्य र न्यायको सुनिश्चितता’ भन्ने नाराका साथ यस वर्षकाे अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय महिला हिंसा अन्त्य दिवस मनाइदै छ । यी नाराहरू केवल औपचारिक कार्यक्रमका लागि तयार गरिएका शब्द होइनन् । यी त समाजमा विद्यमान हिंसा, विभेद, अन्याय र मौनताविरुद्ध उठ्नुपर्ने सामूहिक आवाज हुन् ।

महिलाहरुमाथि हुने हिंसा : देखिने घाउभन्दा गहिरो हुन्छ नदेखिने पीडा

महिला हिंसा भन्नासाथ धेरैलाई कुटपिट, शारीरिक आक्रमण वा बलात्कारजस्ता घटनाको मात्र स्मरण हुन्छ। तर महिला हिंसा यतिमा मात्र सीमित छैन । शारीरिक, मानसिक, भावनात्मक, यौनजन्य, आर्थिक, सामाजिक तथा डिजिटल माध्यमबाट हुने दुर्व्यवहार र शोषण पनि लैङ्गिक हिंसाकै स्वरूप हुन् ।

हाम्रो समाजमा आज पनि धेरै महिलाहरू आफ्नै घरभित्र असुरक्षित जीवन बिताउन बाध्य छन् । श्रीमान् वा परिवारका सदस्यबाट हुने कुटपिट, गालीगलौज, अपमान, शङ्का, धम्की, इच्छाविपरीत यौनसम्बन्ध राख्न बाध्य पार्ने व्यवहार तथा आर्थिक नियन्त्रण घरेलु हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् ।

कहिलेकाहीँ हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्ति परिवारकै सदस्य, आफन्त, चिनजानको व्यक्ति वा समाजमा प्रतिष्ठित मानिएको व्यक्ति पनि हुन सक्छ। त्यसैले हिंसा केवल अपरिचित व्यक्तिबाट मात्र हुन्छ भन्ने सोच गलत हो ।

त्यस्तै, कार्यस्थलमा हुने यौन दुर्व्यवहार, असमान व्यवहार, समान कामको असमान पारिश्रमिक, अवसरबाट वञ्चित गराउने प्रवृत्ति, सार्वजनिक स्थानमा हुने दुर्व्यवहार र महिलाको चरित्रमाथि प्रश्न उठाउने सामाजिक व्यवहार पनि महिलाको स्वतन्त्रता र सम्मानमाथिका प्रहार हुन् ।

प्रविधिको विकाससँगै महिलामाथि हुने हिंसाका स्वरूप पनि परिवर्तन भएका छन्। सामाजिक सञ्जालमार्फत चरित्रहत्या गर्ने, अश्लील तथा आपत्तिजनक सन्देश पठाउने, अनुमति नलिई निजी तस्बिर सार्वजनिक गर्ने, फोटो तथा भिडियो दुरुपयोग गर्ने, अनलाइन धम्की दिने र साइबर बुलिङ गर्ने घटनाहरू बढ्दो चिन्ताको विषय बनेका छन् ।

अझै पनि बालविवाह, दाइजो प्रथा, छाउपडी, बोक्सीको आरोप, मानव बेचबिखन, जबर्जस्ती विवाह तथा छोरा र छोरीबीच गरिने विभेदले महिलाको जीवन, स्वास्थ्य, शिक्षा र आत्मसम्मानमा गम्भीर असर पारिरहेका छन् ।

हिंसा सहनु महिलाको बाध्यता होइन, हिंसा गर्नु अपराध हो

हिंसामा परेका महिलाहरू किन बोल्दैनन् ? किन न्याय खोज्न अगाडि आउँदैनन् ? भन्ने प्रश्न समाजले बारम्बार उठाउँछ । तर उनीहरूको मौनताभित्र लुकेका बाध्यता बुझ्ने प्रयास कमै गरिन्छ ।

परिवार टुट्ने डर, आर्थिक परनिर्भरता, बालबालिकाको भविष्यको चिन्ता, सामाजिक प्रतिष्ठा गुम्ने भय, माइती तथा आफन्तबाट साथ नपाउने अवस्था, समाजले लगाउने लाञ्छना र न्याय प्राप्त गर्न लाग्ने समय तथा प्रक्रियाको जटिलताले धेरै महिलालाई हिंसा सहेर बस्न बाध्य बनाउँछ ।

कतिपय महिलाले आफ्नै पीडा व्यक्त गर्दा उल्टै दोषी ठहरिनुपर्छ । उनीहरूको पहिरन, व्यवहार, बोलचाल, चरित्र र व्यक्तिगत जीवनमाथि प्रश्न उठाइन्छ । हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिभन्दा हिंसामा परेकी महिलालाई नै समाजले स्पष्टीकरण माग्ने अवस्था अझै विद्यमान छ ।

हामीले बुझ्नुपर्छ, हिंसाको जिम्मेवारी हिंसा गर्ने व्यक्तिको हो, पीडितको होइन । कुनै पनि महिलाको पहिरन, स्वतन्त्रता, व्यक्तिगत निर्णय वा जीवनशैली हिंसाको औचित्य बन्न सक्दैन ।

न्याय केवल कानुनमा होइन, व्यवहारमा पनि सुनिश्चित हुनुपर्छ

महिला हिंसा अन्त्यका लागि कानुन निर्माण गर्नु मात्र पर्याप्त हुँदैन । कानुनको प्रभावकारी कार्यान्वयन, निष्पक्ष अनुसन्धान, पीडितमैत्री न्याय प्रणाली, गोपनीयताको संरक्षण र दोषीलाई कानुनअनुसार कारबाही गर्नु उत्तिकै आवश्यक छ ।

हिंसामा परेका महिलालाई तत्काल सुरक्षा, आवश्यक स्वास्थ्य सेवा, मनोसामाजिक परामर्श, कानुनी सहायता, सुरक्षित आवास र आर्थिक तथा सामाजिक पुनर्स्थापनाको व्यवस्था हुनुपर्छ ।

पीडितले न्याय खोज्दा बारम्बार आफ्नो पीडा सुनाउनुपर्ने, अपमान सहनुपर्ने वा सामाजिक रूपमा थप प्रताडित हुनुपर्ने अवस्था अन्त्य गरिनुपर्छ। उनीहरूको पहिचान र गोपनीयता सुरक्षित राख्दै सम्मानजनक व्यवहार गर्नु राज्य, सेवा प्रदायक निकाय र समाज सबैको दायित्व हो ।

यस वर्षको अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय नाराले पनि यही सन्देश दिएको छ-पीडितलाई संरक्षण गरौँ, न्याय सुनिश्चित गरौँ र अपराध गर्ने व्यक्तिले उन्मुक्ति पाउने दण्डहीनताको संस्कृतिको अन्त्य गरौँ ।

महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्न हाम्रो भूमिका के हुन सक्छ ?

महिला हिंसा अन्त्य गर्नु सरकार वा कुनै एक संस्थाको मात्र जिम्मेवारी होइन । परिवार, विद्यालय, समुदाय, सञ्चारमाध्यम, स्थानीय तह, स्वास्थ्य संस्था, सुरक्षा निकाय र प्रत्येक नागरिकको साझा दायित्व हाे।

महिलाको सुरक्षा र सम्मान, स्वस्थ समाजको आधार

महिला परिवार, समाज र राष्ट्र निर्माणका महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । घरपरिवारको व्यवस्थापनदेखि शिक्षा, स्वास्थ्य, कृषि, उद्योग, व्यवसाय, प्रशासन, राजनीति र विकासका हरेक क्षेत्रमा महिलाको योगदान अतुलनीय छ । तर विडम्बना, आजको आधुनिक र प्रविधिमैत्री समाजमा समेत महिलाले आफ्नो अस्तित्व, स्वतन्त्रता, सम्मान र सुरक्षाका लागि संघर्ष गर्नुपर्ने अवस्था पूर्ण रूपमा अन्त्य हुन सकेको छैन ।

महिलामाथि हुने हिंसा केवल कुटपिट, बलात्कार वा शारीरिक आक्रमणमा सीमित छैन। मानसिक यातना, अपमान, आर्थिक नियन्त्रण, सामाजिक विभेद, यौन दुर्व्यवहार, कार्यस्थलमा हुने शोषण र पछिल्लो समय बढ्दै गएको डिजिटल हिंसा पनि यसकै स्वरूप हुन् ।

विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले महिला हिंसालाई मानव अधिकार उल्लङ्घनका साथै एउटा गम्भीर सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य समस्याका रूपमा व्याख्या गरेको छ ।

किनकि हिंसाले महिलाको शरीरमा चोट पुर्‍याउने मात्र होइन, मानसिक स्वास्थ्य, यौन तथा प्रजनन स्वास्थ्य, पारिवारिक सम्बन्ध, सामाजिक जीवन र समग्र जीवनको गुणस्तरमा दीर्घकालीन असर पार्दछ।

महिला हिंसाको विश्वव्यापी अवस्था : अनुसन्धानले देखाएको वास्तविकता

महिला हिंसाको अवस्था बुझ्न विभिन्न राष्ट्रिय तथा अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय अनुसन्धान र तथ्याङ्क महत्त्वपूर्ण आधार हुन् । विश्व स्वास्थ्य सङ्गठनले नोभेम्बर २०२५ मा सार्वजनिक गरेको पछिल्लो विश्वव्यापी प्रतिवेदनअनुसार संसारभर करिब ८४ करोड महिला अर्थात् झन्डै तीनमध्ये एक महिलाले आफ्नो जीवनकालमा अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसा अथवा अन्य व्यक्तिबाट हुने यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् ।

त्यस्तै, पछिल्लो केहि महिनामा यता मात्रै विश्वभर करिब ३१ करोड ६० लाख महिला अन्तरंग साथीबाट हुने शारीरिक वा यौन हिंसाबाट प्रभावित भएको अनुमान छ ।

यी तथ्याङ्कले महिला हिंसा कुनै एक देश, समुदाय वा आर्थिक वर्गको मात्र समस्या नभई विश्वव्यापी स्वास्थ्य तथा मानव अधिकारको चुनौती भएको स्पष्ट पार्छन्।

नेपालको अवस्था पनि यसबाट अलग छैन । नेपाल जनसाङ्ख्यिक तथा स्वास्थ्य सर्वेक्षणअनुसार १५ देखि ४९ वर्ष उमेर समूहका २३ प्रतिशत महिलाले १५ वर्षको उमेरपछि कुनै न कुनै प्रकारको शारीरिक हिंसा अनुभव गरेका छन् भने ८ प्रतिशत महिलाले जीवनकालमा यौन हिंसाको अनुभव गरेका छन् ।

त्यस्तै, श्रीमान् वा अन्तरङ्ग साथीसँग सम्बन्धमा रहेका महिलामध्ये २७ प्रतिशतले शारीरिक, यौनजन्य वा भावनात्मक हिंसाको अनुभव गरेको सर्वेक्षणले देखाएको छ ।

यी तथ्याङ्क केवल प्रतिशत होइनन्, हाम्रै समाजमा हिंसा र असुरक्षाबीच जीवन बिताउन बाध्य महिलाहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व हुन् ।

महिला हिंसाका प्रमुख स्वरूपहरू

क) शारीरिक हिंसा

महिलामाथि गरिने कुटपिट, लात्ती तथा मुक्का प्रहार, जलाउने, घाँटी थिच्ने, चोटपटक पुर्‍याउने, खानपिन वा औषधोपचारबाट वञ्चित गर्ने तथा ज्यान मार्ने धम्की दिने कार्य शारीरिक हिंसाका उदाहरण हुन् ।

विशेषगरी घरभित्र हुने हिंसालाई पारिवारिक विषय भन्दै लुकाउने प्रवृत्तिले धेरै महिला वर्षौँसम्म शारीरिक यातना सहन बाध्य हुन्छन् ।

यस्ता हिंसाले चोटपटक, हड्डी भाँचिने, आन्तरिक रक्तस्राव, दीर्घकालीन दुखाइ, अपाङ्गता र कतिपय अवस्थामा मृत्युसमेत निम्त्याउन सक्छ ।

ख) मानसिक तथा मनोवैज्ञानिक हिंसा

महिलालाई निरन्तर गाली गर्नु, अपमानित गर्नु, चरित्रमाथि शंका गर्नु, डर देखाउनु, धम्की दिनु, अरूसँग बोल्न तथा भेटघाट गर्न रोक्नु, इच्छाविपरीत निर्णय लाद्नु र आत्मसम्मान कमजोर बनाउने व्यवहार मानसिक हिंसा हुन् । यसको असर बाहिरबाट देखिँदैन, तर भित्रभित्रै महिलाको आत्मविश्वास र मानसिक स्वास्थ्य कमजोर बनाउँदै लैजान्छ ।

यस्ता महिलामा चिन्ता, अवसाद, तनाव, निद्रासम्बन्धी समस्या र आघातपछिको मानसिक तनाव जस्ता समस्या देखिन सक्छन् ।

ग) यौनजन्य हिंसा

Every year, November 25 is observed as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. From this day until December 10, International Human Rights Day, a 16-day campaign against gender-based violence is launched worldwide. This campaign aims to end all forms of violence against women, ensure the rights of victims and affected people, and build a society free from violence. This year's International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is being celebrated with the theme 'Unity to End Gender-Based Violence: Protecting Victims, Ending Impunity and Ensuring Justice'. These themes are not just words prepared for formal events. They are a collective voice that must rise up against the violence, discrimination, injustice and silence that exist in society. Violence against women: The unseen pain is deeper than the visible wound When it comes to violence against women, many people only think of incidents like beatings, physical attacks, or rape. But violence against women is not limited to these. Abuse and exploitation that occur through physical, mental, emotional, sexual, economic, social, and digital means are also forms of gender-based violence. Even today, many women in our society are forced to live unsafe lives within their own homes. Examples of domestic violence include beatings, verbal abuse, humiliation, suspicion, threats, coercive sexual behavior against one's will, and financial control by a husband or family member. Sometimes the perpetrator of violence can be a family member, relative, acquaintance, or even a person considered respected in society. Therefore, it is wrong to think that violence only occurs from strangers. Similarly, sexual harassment in the workplace, unequal treatment, unequal pay for equal work, the tendency to deprive women of opportunities, abuse in public places, and social behavior that questions women's character are also attacks on women's freedom and dignity. With the development of technology, the forms of violence against women have also changed. Incidents of character assassination, sending obscene and offensive messages through social media, publishing private photos without permission, misusing photos and videos, online threats, and cyberbullying have become a matter of growing concern. Child marriage, dowry system, Chhaupadi, witchcraft accusations, human trafficking, forced marriage, and discrimination between sons and daughters still have a serious impact on women's lives, health, education, and self-esteem. It is not a woman's obligation to endure violence, committing violence is a crime. Society repeatedly raises the question of why women who are victims of violence don't speak out? Why don't they come forward to seek justice? But rarely does an effort to understand the hidden compulsions behind their silence occur. Fear of family breakdown, financial dependence, concerns about the future of children, fear of losing social prestige, lack of support from family and relatives, stigmatization by society, and the time and complexity of the process required to obtain justice force many women to endure violence. Some women are accused of expressing their pain. Their dress, behavior, speech, character, and personal lives are questioned. Society still demands an explanation from the woman who is the victim of violence rather than the person who commits the violence. We must understand that the responsibility for violence lies with the perpetrator, not the victim. No woman's dress, freedom, personal decisions, or lifestyle can justify violence. Justice must be ensured not only in law, but also in practice. Enacting laws alone is not enough to end violence against women. Effective implementation of the law, impartial investigations, a victim-friendly justice system, protection of confidentiality, and prosecution of perpetrators according to the law are equally necessary. Women who have been subjected to violence should be provided with immediate protection, necessary health services, psychosocial counseling, legal assistance, safe housing, and economic and social rehabilitation. Victims should not have to repeatedly recount their pain, endure humiliation, or be further socially harassed when seeking justice. It is the responsibility of the state, service providers, and society to protect their identity and privacy and treat them with respect. This year's international slogan also conveys the same message - protect victims, ensure justice, and end the culture of impunity where perpetrators of crimes get away with it. What can be our role in ending violence against women? Ending violence against women is not the sole responsibility of the government or any single organization. It is a shared responsibility of families, schools, communities, media, local levels, health institutions, security agencies, and every citizen. Women's safety and respect, the foundation of a healthy society Women are the important foundation of family, society and nation building. From household management to education, health, agriculture, industry, business, administration, politics and development, women's contribution is unparalleled. But ironically, even in today's modern and technology-friendly society, the situation where women have to struggle for their existence, freedom, respect and security has not been completely eliminated. Violence against women is not limited to beatings, rape, or physical attacks. It also includes mental torture, humiliation, economic control, social discrimination, sexual abuse, workplace exploitation, and the recent rise in digital violence. The World Health Organization has described violence against women as a human rights violation as well as a serious public health problem. Because violence not only harms women's bodies, it also has long-term impacts on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, family relationships, social life, and overall quality of life. The global state of violence against women: The reality revealed by research Various national and international research and statistics are an important basis for understanding the situation of violence against women. According to the latest global report released by the World Health Organization in November 2025, about 840 million women worldwide, or about one in three women, have experienced physical or sexual violence from an intimate partner or sexual violence from another person in their lifetime. Similarly, in the last few months alone, it is estimated that approximately 316 million women worldwide have been affected by physical or sexual violence from intimate partners. These statistics make it clear that violence against women is not just a problem of one country, community, or economic class, but a global health and human rights challenge. Nepal is no different. According to the Nepal Demographic and Health Survey, 23 percent of women aged 15 to 49 have experienced some form of physical violence after the age of 15, while 8 percent have experienced sexual violence in their lifetime. Similarly, the survey showed that 27 percent of women in relationships with their husbands or intimate partners have experienced physical, sexual, or emotional violence. These statistics are not just percentages, they are a representation of the women forced to live amidst violence and insecurity in our society. Main forms of violence against women a) Physical violence Examples of physical violence against women include beating, kicking and punching, burning, strangling, causing injuries, depriving them of food, drink or medication, and threatening to kill them. Many women are forced to endure years of physical abuse, especially due to the tendency to hide domestic violence as a family matter. Such violence can cause injuries, broken bones, internal bleeding, chronic pain, disability, and in some cases even death. b) Mental and psychological violence Constantly insulting, humiliating, questioning a woman's character, instilling fear, threatening, preventing her from speaking to or meeting others, imposing decisions against her will, and behavior that undermines her self-esteem are all forms of mental violence. Its effects are not visible from the outside, but they undermine a woman's self-confidence and mental health from the inside. Such women may experience problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, sleep problems, and post-traumatic stress disorder. c) Sexual violence Examples of this include sexual behavior against a woman's will, rape, sexual abuse, unwanted touching, sexual exploitation, forced sexual intercourse, and sexual intimidation. This can lead to unwanted pregnancies, risk of sexually transmitted infections, psychological trauma, and reproductive health complications. Consent is essential in sexual relations. A woman's right to consent does not end just because she is married. Silence or fear cannot be considered consent. d) Economic violence Taking away the money a woman earns, preventing her from spending her income, depriving her of property rights, preventing her from getting a job, and not participating in financial decisions are examples of economic violence. Economic dependence makes it difficult for women to leave violent relationships. Women's education, employment, skill development, and economic self-reliance are important foundations for preventing violence. e) Social and cultural violence Disappointment at the birth of a girl child, discrimination between sons and daughters, demand for dowry, child marriage, untouchability during menstruation, discrimination against widows and single women, and restrictions on women's freedom are all forms of social violence. There is a need to change the mindset that considers injustice against women in the name of tradition and culture as normal. f) Violence in the workplace Women face various forms of abuse not only at home, but also in hospitals, schools, government offices, private organizations, industries, and other workplaces. Unwanted personal comments, derogatory comments about the body, obscene jokes, unwanted touching, pressure for sexual intercourse, sexual demands under the guise of a job or promotion, and retaliation after reporting are examples of workplace violence. Abuse, especially through abuse of position and power, can weaken women mentally and affect their professional lives. There should be a safe environment in the office, a confidential complaint system, and an impartial investigation. g) Digital violence With the development of technology, the forms of violence against women have also changed. Examples of digital violence include character assassination on social media, sending obscene messages, creating fake accounts, publishing personal photos and videos without permission, online threats, blackmailing, and using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create fake obscene photos and videos. Digital Violence should not be treated as a simple joke or an online dispute. It can seriously affect women's mental health, social reputation, and personal safety. Violence against women and its impact on health From the perspective of health professionals, violence against women is not just a social problem, it is a serious condition that affects the overall health of women. Women affected by violence can experience both immediate and long-term health problems. Physical health: Injuries, broken bones, chronic pain, headaches, digestive system problems, and other physical complications. Mental health: Anxiety, stress, depression, fear, loss of confidence, sleep problems, and suicide risk. Sexual and reproductive health: Unwanted pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, risk of HIV infection, pregnancy complications, and reproductive health problems. Maternal and Child Health: Violence against pregnant women can negatively impact the health of both the mother and the unborn child. It can also affect the mental health, behavior, and academic achievement of children who grow up witnessing violence at home. Research by the World Health Organization has shown that the effects of violence can last long after the incident has ended. Therefore, women affected by violence need not only physical treatment, but also mental health services, psychosocial counseling, and social rehabilitation. The role of healthcare workers: trust and protection along with treatment The role of health workers in the prevention and management of violence against women is very important. A woman who has experienced violence may first go to a hospital or health facility without going to the police or court. She may come to a health facility with injuries, headaches, stomachaches, sleep problems, mental stress, or other health problems. Therefore, healthcare workers must be sensitive to the patient's external symptoms as well as their safety, mental state, and possible background of violence. The following should be prioritized in health services: Communicate with the patient in a safe and confidential environment. Listen carefully to the victim. No accusations or insults of any kind. Perform necessary physical examinations and treatment. Providing mental health and psychosocial support. Provide timely necessary health services in cases of sexual violence. Referral to legal and social protection services as needed. Maintaining patient personal details and confidentiality. The World Health Organization has recommended the LIVES Approach as an initial step in providing support to women affected by violence. L – Listen: Listen carefully. I – Inquire: Understand their needs and concerns. V – Validate: Trust and acknowledge their experience. E – Enhance Safety: Help ensure safety. S – Support: Providing necessary services and support. Its primary purpose is not to control the victim, but to strengthen their confidence, security, and decision-making abilities. A new research-based concept in violence prevention Simply conducting awareness programs is not enough to end violence against women. Research-based policies and programs are needed to prevent it. The RESPECT Women Framework, updated by the World Health Organization in 2025, is an important concept for preventing violence against women. It emphasizes seven key strategies Developing healthy and respectful relationships. Women's empowerment. Ensuring health, legal and social services. Reducing poverty and economic dependence. Making homes, schools and workplaces safe. Preventing abuse of children and adolescents. Changing discriminatory thinking and social norms. This shows that coordination between health, education, economic development, law, and social awareness is necessary to prevent violence against women. Victims need support and justice, not blame. In our society, women who have experienced violence still have to face social humiliation and mental stress in addition to physical pain. In some cases, when a victim makes an incident public, questions are raised about their character, dress, behavior, relationships, and personal life. Questions like why did she go there? Why didn't she file a complaint earlier? Why didn't she end the relationship? Why did she keep quiet? cause further mental anguish to the victim. We need to change the direction of the question. Why did the violence happen? Why weren't the perpetrators brought to justice? Why didn't the victims get timely protection and justice? We should develop a culture of listening to the victim, trusting them, maintaining confidentiality, and providing necessary support, rather than blaming them. Survivor Support, not Victim Blaming, should be our priority. The responsibility of family, society and the state to end violence against women The responsibility to end violence against women is not only women's. It is a shared responsibility of families, men, communities, health institutions, educational institutions, the media, and the state. Daughters and sons should be treated equally in the family. The idea that household chores are the sole responsibility of women should be changed. Women's opinions, decisions, and freedom should be respected. Men should also play an active role in combating violence against women. They should not remain silent when they see humiliation, discrimination, and abuse against women. Health institutions should provide safe, confidential, and victim-friendly services for women affected by violence. Offices and organizations should create a safe work environment and an effective complaint mechanism. The state should prioritize effective implementation of existing laws, impartial investigations, speedy justice, safe havens, free legal aid, and rehabilitation programs.* : Ensuring legal order and justice in Nepal: The Constitution of Nepal, 2072 BS, ensures the rights of women to equality, respect, and security. Similarly, legal provisions such as the Domestic Violence (Offences and Punishments) Act, 2066 BS, the Sexual Harassment at Workplace (Prevention) Act, 2071 BS, and the Criminal Code, 2074 BS have addressed various forms of violence against women and girls. But laws alone are not enough. They must be effectively implemented. Victims should receive fair investigation, a safe environment, health care, legal aid, and timely justice after filing a complaint. The perpetrator of violence, no matter how politically, economically, or socially powerful, cannot be above the law. This year's national slogan also emphasizes the same theme - protecting victims, ending impunity, and ensuring justice. Conclusion: Building a violence-free society is our shared responsibility. The campaign to end violence against women should not be limited to a one-day event or a formal 16-day activity. It is a social campaign that must continue every day, in every home, every office, every school, and every community. We must build a society where families are not disappointed when a girl is born, women do not feel unsafe in their own homes, teenagers do not have to give up their dreams, employees do not have to endure humiliation to keep their jobs, and women who have experienced violence do not have to feel alone when seeking justice. Women's safety is not just a personal need of women, but a criterion for the civilization of society and the development of the nation. As a health worker, I believe that a violence-free environment, safe health care, protection of mental health, and equal rights are the foundations of building a healthy society. Let us all make a common commitment on the occasion of this campaign. Let us not remain silent when we see violence. Let us not blame the victim. Let us not consider injustice normal. Let us not protect the perpetrators of violence. Let us raise our voices in favor of justice and equality. Because the vision of a healthy, prosperous, and civilized society remains incomplete until the safety, respect, and health of women are ensured. Women are not obligated to endure violence. Consent is the basis of every relationship. Women's respect and security are fundamental rights. Victims need not only sympathy, but justice and protection. Perpetrators of violence need legal accountability, not impunity. Let us raise our voices, support the victims, and ensure justice. (The author works at Shukraraj Tropical and Infectious Diseases Hospital.)

Such women may experience problems such as anxiety, depression, stress, sleep problems, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

c) Sexual violence

Examples of this include sexual behavior against a woman's will, rape, sexual abuse, unwanted touching, sexual exploitation, forced sexual intercourse, and sexual intimidation.

This can lead to unwanted pregnancies, risk of sexually transmitted infections, psychological trauma, and reproductive health complications.

Consent is essential in sexual relations. A woman's right to consent does not end just because she is married. Silence or fear cannot be considered consent.

d) Economic violence

Taking away the money a woman earns, preventing her from spending her income, depriving her of property rights, preventing her from getting a job, and not participating in financial decisions are examples of economic violence.

Economic dependence makes it difficult for women to leave violent relationships. Women's education, employment, skill development, and economic self-reliance are important foundations for preventing violence.

e) Social and cultural violence

Disappointment at the birth of a girl child, discrimination between sons and daughters, demand for dowry, child marriage, untouchability during menstruation, discrimination against widows and single women, and restrictions on women's freedom are all forms of social violence. There is a need to change the mindset that considers injustice against women in the name of tradition and culture as normal.

f) Violence in the workplace

Women face various forms of abuse not only at home, but also in hospitals, schools, government offices, private organizations, industries, and other workplaces.

Unwanted personal comments, derogatory comments about the body, obscene jokes, unwanted touching, pressure for sexual intercourse, sexual demands under the guise of a job or promotion, and retaliation after reporting are examples of workplace violence.

Abuse, especially through abuse of position and power, can weaken women mentally and affect their professional lives. There should be a safe environment in the office, a confidential complaint system, and an impartial investigation.

g) Digital violence

With the development of technology, the forms of violence against women have also changed.

Examples of digital violence include character assassination on social media, sending obscene messages, creating fake accounts, publishing personal photos and videos without permission, online threats, blackmailing, and using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create fake obscene photos and videos.

Digital Violence should not be treated as a simple joke or an online dispute. It can seriously affect women's mental health, social reputation, and personal safety.

Violence against women and its impact on health

From the perspective of health professionals, violence against women is not just a social problem, it is a serious condition that affects the overall health of women. Women affected by violence can experience both immediate and long-term health problems.

Physical health: Injuries, broken bones, chronic pain, headaches, digestive system problems, and other physical complications.

Mental health: Anxiety, stress, depression, fear, loss of confidence, sleep problems, and suicide risk.

Sexual and reproductive health: Unwanted pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, risk of HIV infection, pregnancy complications, and reproductive health problems.

Maternal and Child Health: Violence against pregnant women can negatively impact the health of both the mother and the unborn child. It can also affect the mental health, behavior, and academic achievement of children who grow up witnessing violence at home.

Research by the World Health Organization has shown that the effects of violence can last long after the incident has ended.

Therefore, women affected by violence need not only physical treatment, but also mental health services, psychosocial counseling, and social rehabilitation.

The role of healthcare workers: trust and protection along with treatment

The role of health workers in the prevention and management of violence against women is very important. A woman who has experienced violence may first go to a hospital or health facility without going to the police or court. She may come to a health facility with injuries, headaches, stomachaches, sleep problems, mental stress, or other health problems.

Therefore, healthcare workers must be sensitive to the patient's external symptoms as well as their safety, mental state, and possible background of violence.

The World Health Organization has recommended the LIVES Approach as an initial step in providing support to women affected by violence.

Its primary purpose is not to control the victim, but to strengthen their confidence, security, and decision-making abilities.

A new research-based concept in violence prevention

Simply conducting awareness programs is not enough to end violence against women. Research-based policies and programs are needed to prevent it.

The RESPECT Women Framework, updated by the World Health Organization in 2025, is an important concept for preventing violence against women.

It emphasizes seven key strategies

This shows that coordination between health, education, economic development, law, and social awareness is necessary to prevent violence against women.

Victims need support and justice, not blame. In our society, women who have experienced violence still have to face social humiliation and mental stress in addition to physical pain.

In some cases, when a victim makes an incident public, questions are raised about their character, dress, behavior, relationships, and personal life.

Questions like why did she go there? Why didn't she file a complaint earlier? Why didn't she end the relationship? Why did she keep quiet? cause further mental anguish to the victim.

We need to change the direction of the question. Why did the violence happen? Why weren't the perpetrators brought to justice? Why didn't the victims get timely protection and justice?

We should develop a culture of listening to the victim, trusting them, maintaining confidentiality, and providing necessary support, rather than blaming them.

Survivor Support, not Victim Blaming, should be our priority.

The responsibility of family, society and the state to end violence against women

The responsibility to end violence against women is not only women's. It is a shared responsibility of families, men, communities, health institutions, educational institutions, the media, and the state.

Daughters and sons should be treated equally in the family. The idea that household chores are the sole responsibility of women should be changed. Women's opinions, decisions, and freedom should be respected.

Men should also play an active role in combating violence against women. They should not remain silent when they see humiliation, discrimination, and abuse against women.

Health institutions should provide safe, confidential, and victim-friendly services for women affected by violence.

Offices and organizations should create a safe work environment and an effective complaint mechanism.

The state should prioritize effective implementation of existing laws, impartial investigations, speedy justice, safe havens, free legal aid, and rehabilitation programs.* : Ensuring legal order and justice in Nepal:

The Constitution of Nepal, 2072 BS, ensures the rights of women to equality, respect, and security.

Similarly, legal provisions such as the Domestic Violence (Offences and Punishments) Act, 2066 BS, the Sexual Harassment at Workplace (Prevention) Act, 2071 BS, and the Criminal Code, 2074 BS have addressed various forms of violence against women and girls. But laws alone are not enough. They must be effectively implemented.

Victims should receive fair investigation, a safe environment, health care, legal aid, and timely justice after filing a complaint. The perpetrator of violence, no matter how politically, economically, or socially powerful, cannot be above the law.

This year's national slogan also emphasizes the same theme - protecting victims, ending impunity, and ensuring justice.

Conclusion: Building a violence-free society is our shared responsibility. The campaign to end violence against women should not be limited to a one-day event or a formal 16-day activity. It is a social campaign that must continue every day, in every home, every office, every school, and every community.

We must build a society where families are not disappointed when a girl is born, women do not feel unsafe in their own homes, teenagers do not have to give up their dreams, employees do not have to endure humiliation to keep their jobs, and women who have experienced violence do not have to feel alone when seeking justice.

Women's safety is not just a personal need of women, but a criterion for the civilization of society and the development of the nation. As a health worker, I believe that a violence-free environment, safe health care, protection of mental health, and equal rights are the foundations of building a healthy society.

Let us all make a common commitment on the occasion of this campaign. Let us not remain silent when we see violence. Let us not blame the victim. Let us not consider injustice normal. Let us not protect the perpetrators of violence. Let us raise our voices in favor of justice and equality. Because the vision of a healthy, prosperous, and civilized society remains incomplete until the safety, respect, and health of women are ensured.

Women are not obligated to endure violence. Consent is the basis of every relationship. Women's respect and security are fundamental rights. Victims need not only sympathy, but justice and protection. Perpetrators of violence need legal accountability, not impunity. Let us raise our voices, support the victims, and ensure justice.
